skillSays: It is a pipeline for turning AI-generated video or frame sequences into web animation driven by scroll, pointer, drag, audio, data or time.
Start by locking a concept contract: driver, time_control (scrub, segment-play or autonomous), input semantics, rest state and reduced-motion state.
Keep timing in one manifest (states, segments, hold times). Pages and controllers read it and never keep a second set of constants.
Pick the delivery format (alpha atlas, chroma video, baked video) and the runtime controller separately, via a budget script.
Pilot first on the real page, then QA reverse playback, cold cache, DPR, mobile and failure cases.
It explicitly declines pure CSS/JS interface transitions and micro-interactions and hands those to ordinary front-end code.

changes: The skill's own scope rule marks a toast as plain UI motion, so no AI media was generated (the pipeline also needs a ZenMux key); only its contract and manifest ideas were applied
All timing sits in one TL manifest of segments (start, end, curve) and render(t) is a pure function of time, so the page keeps no second timeline
An autonomous controller advances t on requestAnimationFrame and loops; reduced motion renders the manifest's rest state once and hides Replay
Same out-of-scope outcome as motion-1: built as ordinary front-end code, with the skill's controller and manifest structure as the only borrowed parts
Cursor travel, menu open, item stagger, highlight steps and close are separate manifest segments with named curves, rendered together from one t
Because render(t) is deterministic the sequence can be seeked and replayed from any frame without state to reset
Out of scope for the skill (UI micro-interaction): no generated media, manifest-driven vanilla JS instead
Typing, add, two check-offs and two removals are segments; row positions are derived from removal progress, so rows below slide up by transform only
Rest state is defined up front (a stable mid-sequence frame) and used as the reduced-motion view
